bib.title: BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions

question: How hard are naturally occurring yes/no questions for reading comprehension, and which transfer-learning sources best help models answer them?
hypothesis: Naturally occurring yes/no questions require difficult entailment-like inference, so entailment data should transfer better than paraphrase or extractive QA data (stated in the abstract as a finding; MultiNLI's contradiction examples are hypothesised as the key advantage).
contributions: BoolQ, a reading comprehension dataset of 16k naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with Wikipedia paragraphs
Analysis of question topics, types and required inference
Transfer-learning baselines comparing entailment, extractive QA, multiple-choice QA, paraphrase, heuristic yes/no and unsupervised pre-training sources

method.summary: Questions come from anonymised Google search queries filtered by first-word heuristics, kept if a Wikipedia page is in the top five results, then annotated for goodness, answer passage and yes/no. Baselines fine-tune recurrent, ELMo, GPT and BERT-large models, with and without supervised pre-training on other datasets.

datasets.name: BoolQ
datasets.size: 16k questions (13k from NQ-style pipeline + 3k yes/no questions from NQ train)
datasets.split: 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, 3.2k test; NQ questions always in train; 62.31% yes in train
datasets.source: Anonymised Google queries, Wikipedia passages, annotated by humans (NQ pipeline)
datasets.preprocessing: Only questions marked yes/no kept; paired with the selected passage rather than the whole document; avg question 8.9 tokens, passage 108 tokens; article title included but unused

datasets.name: MultiNLI
datasets.preprocessing: Probability of entailment class used as probability of yes; ablations drop one class (262k)

datasets.name: RACE
datasets.preprocessing: Questions + options converted to statements; softmax over statements per question; negative log prob of correct statement

datasets.name: SQuAD 2.0 (entailment-like)
datasets.preprocessing: Question concatenated with correct answer or distractor; classify which

datasets.name: NQ Long Answer
datasets.preprocessing: Only questions with an answer; one answer-containing paragraph plus up to 15 random non-answer paragraphs; softmax over paragraphs

datasets.name: Y/N MS Marco
datasets.preprocessing: Answers starting with yes or no, paired with related snippets; 80% yes

models.name: Recurrent
models.architecture: char CNN + fasttext embeddings, BiLSTM, co-attention, BiLSTM, attention pool, FC

models.name: BERT-large
models.init_from: Devlin et al. 2018, Book Corpus and Wikipedia; optionally fine-tuned on MultiNLI first

training.objective: Binary: sigmoid of score on (question, passage) for yes; entailment-class probability for NLI-pretrained models; GPT adds language-model loss weight 0.5
training.optimizer: Adam for the Recurrent model; 'optimizers recommended by the authors' for BERT and GPT (not named)
training.lr_schedule: Recurrent: decayed by 0.999 every 100 steps; BERT/GPT not stated
training.epochs: BERT 5 (3 when pre-trained on MultiNLI); GPT 3
training.seeds: 5 runs per model; pretraining and fine-tuning both repeated for supervised sources; Table 4 reports the run with best dev accuracy

other.unsupervised_pretraining_data: ELMo Billion Word 1000M; GPT Books 800M; BERT Books/Wikipedia 3,300M (Table 3)

inference.samples: Table 3 averaged over five runs; Table 4 single best-dev run of five

eval.protocol: Dev accuracy averaged over five runs (Table 3); test accuracy of best-dev run of five seeds (Table 4). Human accuracy from 110 examples labelled by three authors; no significance test.

evidence.quote: We use a batch size of 24, learning rate of 1e-5, and 5 training epochs for BERT

results.claim: Best model (BERT-large pre-trained on MultiNLI then fine-tuned on BoolQ) reaches 80.43% test accuracy.
results.setup: BoolQ test set, BERT-large +MultiNLI, best-dev run of five seeds

results.claim: Human annotators reach about 90% accuracy against gold labels.
results.setup: 110 random examples, three authors labelled and conferred for gold; annotator answers compared to gold
results.quote: the answer annotations reached 90% ac-curacy compared to the gold-standard labels
results.note: Annotators were not the same as the authors who made gold labels; sample of 110.

results.claim: Majority baseline is 62.17% dev and 62.31% test.
results.table: Table 4, row Majority Class, column Test Acc.
results.note: Text also says 62.31% yes in train set; dev majority 62.17%.

results.claim: Pre-trained BERT-large without MultiNLI gets 76.70% test, 78.09% dev.
results.setup: BoolQ test, BERT-large fine-tuned on BoolQ only
results.table: Table 4, row Pre-trained BERT-L, column Test Acc.

results.claim: MultiNLI pre-training adds about 3.5 points on top of BERT-large.
results.quote: the additional gain of 3.5 points due to using MultiNLI is remarkable
results.note: Table 4 differences are 4.11 dev (82.20-78.09) and 3.73 test (80.43-76.70).

results.claim: Recurrent model trained only on BoolQ gets 69.6%, 8% above majority.
results.quote: Our best model reaches 69.6% accuracy, only 8% better than the majority baseline.
results.note: Table 4 gives Recurrent dev 70.28 and test 67.52; Table 3 gives 69.60 averaged over five runs.

results.claim: MultiNLI is the best supervised transfer source for the Recurrent model.
results.setup: BoolQ dev, Recurrent model, averaged over five runs
results.table: Table 3, row MultiNLI, column BoolQ Acc.

results.claim: BERT-large unsupervised pre-training alone gets 76.90% dev.
results.table: Table 3, row BERT-L, column BoolQ Acc.

results.claim: Question-only BERT-large gets 64.48% and passage-only 66.74% dev, near majority 62.17%.
results.quote: The pre-trained BERTL model reached 64.48% dev set accuracy using just the question and 66.74% using just the passage.

results.table: Table 3, row SNLI, column BoolQ Acc.

results.claim: RACE transfer gives no gain over no pre-training.
results.table: Table 3, row RACE, column BoolQ Acc.

results.claim: Removing the contradiction class from MultiNLI drops two-step BERT to 78.43% dev.
results.setup: BERT-large, MultiNLI without contradiction, then BoolQ
results.quote: only reaches 78.43% dev set accuracy if we remove the contradiction class from MultiNLI

results.claim: Less than 40% of examples are solvable by paraphrase detection (paraphrasing 38.7%).
results.setup: Manual categorisation of reasoning types; dataset since updated so possibly out of date

results.claim: Pre-training on MultiNLI gives at least 5-6 points, nearly 10 for BERT-large with 1000 examples.
results.setup: BoolQ dev, varying train size (read from Fig 2)
results.quote: Pre-training on MultiNLI gives at least a 5-6 point gain, and nearly a 10 point gain for BERTL when only using 1000 examples.

limits: Annotation quality checked on only 110 examples; train/dev/test are singly annotated.
Inference-type analysis (Table 2) was done before a dataset update and may be out of date (footnote 4).
Only passages, not whole documents; authors suggest a document-level version as future work.
Table 4 reports the best-dev run of five seeds, not a mean.
Multi-source pre-training combinations were left to future work.
Dated: 2019 baselines (BERT-large, GPT-1, ELMo); modern LLMs not evaluated.
